absent: Access permissions, trapping behavior, readable versus writable roles, and reset values for the listed registers.
Operational semantics of barriers, cache maintenance, trace, branch record, PMU, activity monitors, timers, GIC, debug, and error handling beyond encodings and bit positions.
Locking, concurrency, ordering, context, and calling rules for accessing these registers.
Struct layouts, function contracts, entry points, and state machines that use these registers.
Encodings for remaining second exception level virtual interrupt, list, context, offset, and hypervisor timer names beyond the truncated visible range.

findings.text: Privileged access never state is identified by a system encoding with op0 3, op1 0, CRn 4, CRm 2 and op2 3. Barrier words are formed by combining a fixed high pattern with value D5 followed by zeros with an encoded system field and the low five bits of a selector. The speculation barrier fixes its six fields to 0 then 3 then 3 then 0 then 7 with selector 31, while the two guarded speculation variants fix them to 1 then 0 then 12 then 0 then 0 and to 1 then 0 then 12 then 0 then 1, both with selector 31.

Set and way cache maintenance operations share op0 1 with op1 0 and CRn 7. The CRm field selects the operation class with 6 for invalidate, 10 for clean and 14 for clean plus invalidate. The op2 field selects tag handling with 2 for plain, 4 for tagged and 6 for tagged with data. This yields nine combinations covering the three classes times the three handling modes.

Address based maintenance and instruction cache operations share op0 1 with CRn 7. Invalidate by address uses op1 0 with CRm 6 and op2 1 then 3 then 5 for plain then tagged then tagged with data. Clean to point of coherency and clean plus invalidate use op1 3 with CRm 10 and 14 with the same three op2 steps. Unify, persist and persist with acknowledge use op1 3 with CRm 11, 12 and 13, the latter two with the same three op2 steps. Zero and tag variants use op1 3 with CRm 4 and op2 1 then 3 then 4. Secure clean plus invalidate uses op1 0 with CRm 15 and op2 1 then 5. Instruction cache invalidate all uses op1 0 with CRm 1 for inner shareable and 5 for full, both with op2 0, while invalidate by address to point of unification uses op1 3 with CRm 5 and op2 1.

Streaming mode control uses op0 0 with op1 3 and CRn 4 and op2 3, with CRm 2 for stop, 3 for start and 6 for stop with zeroing. Breakpoint value and control plus watchpoint value and control are parameterized by an index placed directly in CRm, sharing op0 2 with op1 0 and CRn 0 and op2 4 then 5 then 6 then 7 for the four roles. Debug identification, OS lock status, OS double lock, power control, claim set and clear, authentication status, comms status, data transfer and 32 bit vector catch use fixed encodings under op0 2. OS lock modeling uses a mask combining bit 3 with bit 0, with value zero meaning not implemented, bit 3 meaning implemented, and bit 1 as the lock indicator.

Branch record entries are parameterized by an index from 0 to 31, with the low four bits selecting CRm and the fifth bit folded into op2 alongside a base selecting info versus source versus target, all sharing op0 2 with op1 1 and CRn 8.

Embedded trace registers mostly share op0 2 with op1 1. Fixed controls cover programming, status, configuration, trace ID, synchronization, stall, timestamp, cycle count, branch broadcast, event, filtering, sequencing, address and context comparison, OS lock, claim, device discovery and authentication. Identification registers cover versions 0 through 13 plus device architecture and device ID. Indexed comparators, counters, reloads, values, external selectors, resource selectors, single shot controls and status, sequencer events, context and virtual context values map a small index into CRm and op2 with masking and shifting so only low bits affect the encoding. One integration control uses op0 3 with op1 0 and CRn 1 and CRm 2 and op2 3.

Identification, control, key, exception and fault registers use fixed encodings under op0 3 with op1 0. Main ID, multiprocessor ID and revision ID share CRn 0 with CRm 0 and op2 0 then 5 then 6. Auxiliary control, stack tag seed and control share CRn 1 with CRm 0. Pointer authentication keys share CRn 2 with CRm 1 for instruction A, 2 for data halves, and 3 for generic, with op2 selecting low versus high halves. Saved state and link share CRn 4 with CRm 0, interrupt priority mask uses CRn 4 with CRm 6. Fault status, syndrome, error records, tag fault status and address translation result share CRn 5 through 7. One trace OS lock uses op0 2 with op1 1 and CRn 1 and CRm 0 and op2 4. The translation result failure flag is bit 0.

Translation result layout depends on the failure flag. When set, bits 6 down to 1 hold fault status, bit 8 is a walk indicator, bit 9 is a stage indicator, bits 12 through 15 are assured only then top level then overlay then dirty indicators, bit 11 is reserved one, while bit 7 with bit 10 and bits 47 down to 16 are reserved zero and the top 16 bits are implementation defined. When clear, bits 8 down to 7 hold shareability, bit 9 is non secure, bit 10 is implementation defined, bit 11 is realm non secure, bits 51 down to 12 hold physical address, bits 63 down to 56 hold attributes, while bits 6 down to 1 and bits 55 down to 52 are reserved zero.

Profiling and trace buffer status reuse a shared shift and mask for fault and buffer codes, with value one meaning buffer full for the profiling case and a six bit mask starting at zero for the trace case. Performance interrupt set and clear plus module identification, memory attribute, vector base and deferred interrupt status use fixed encodings. Interrupt controller CPU interface registers for acknowledge, end of interrupt, highest pending, priority, active priority, deactivate, running priority, software generated, control, system register enable and group enable use fixed encodings, with active priority banks parameterized by a two bit index folded into op2 and fixed aliases for values 0 through 3.

Accelerator data, counter kernel control and auxiliary ID use fixed encodings. Random number generation uses two adjacent op2 values under shared CRn and CRm. Performance counting at user level shares op0 3 with op1 3 and CRn 9, with CRm 12 through 14 selecting control versus enable versus overflow versus software increment versus identification versus cycle versus selected event versus user enable. Thread ID, read only thread ID, second thread ID and context number share CRn 13 with CRm 0 and op2 2 then 3 then 5 then 7.

Activity monitoring builds on a base with op0 3 and op1 3 and CRn 13 where the caller supplies CRm and op2. Control, configuration, global control, user enable and first and second bank enable set and clear use CRm 2 and 3 with low op2 values. Per counter value and type for both banks map an index by shifting high bits into CRm and masking low three bits into op2, with separate CRm bases for value versus type and for first versus second bank. Fixed aliases select group zero indices 0 through 3 for core then constant then instructions retired then memory stall.

Generic timer frequency, physical and virtual counts and secure snapshots, plus physical and virtual timer value, control and compare use fixed encodings under op0 3 with op1 3 and CRn 14, with AArch32 aliases under op0 0. Performance event counters and types map an index by masking low three bits into op2 and folding next bits into CRm with distinct bases for counters versus types and for EL1 snapshot versus EL0 access. Cycle filter and partitioned control use fixed encodings. Partitioned event counters, filters and types map a page selector plus index into CRm with low three index bits into op2.

Second exception level controls for virtual ID, auxiliary control, second control, hypervisor configuration, debug, trap, string and access, translation bases and controls, saved state, stack pointer, banked status for interrupt abort undefined and fast interrupt, fault status and syndrome, virtual syndrome, floating point exception, tag fault, fault address and hypervisor fault address, memory attributes, vector bases, reset management and deferred interrupt use fixed encodings under op0 3 with op1 4. Virtual active priority banks for groups 0 and 1 are parameterized by a two bit selector in op2 with fixed aliases for 0 through 3.

Indexed encodings mask their inputs before placement, so only the stated low bits influence CRm or op2 and higher bits are ignored. Direct indices place the masked value in CRm, while wider indices split low bits into CRm and high bits into op2, and banked aliases equal the parameterized form applied to constants 0 through 3.

Several names denote the same encoding and must be treated as aliases. Debug transfer receive and transmit share one encoding so direction comes from the access not the name. Profiling fault and buffer status share shift and mask values. Fixed active priority, activity counter and similar aliases expand to the same encodings as their parameterized forms, so a write through one name is visible through the other.
